lines.say: A hundred million users, and your app finds your account in milliseconds. Now drop one email index. The same logins can take seconds.
lines.show: *100 million* users, and your app finds your account in *milliseconds.* Now drop one email index. The same logins can take *seconds.*

lines.say: Your users live in one big table, one row each, in no order. Without an index, the database may scan the entire table, row after row. A hundred million rows to read, on every login.
lines.show: Your users live in one big table, *one row each,* in no order. Without an index, the database may scan the *entire table,* row after row. *100 million rows* to read, [on every login.]

lines.say: The fix: one line of SQL builds an index: a separate list of one column, like email, kept sorted. Each entry points back to its row.
lines.show: The fix is one line of SQL that builds an [index:] a separate list of one column, like email, kept *sorted.* Each entry *points* back to its row.

lines.say: Because it's sorted, the database doesn't start at the top. It jumps to the S section, narrows it down in a few hops, and lands on your exact row.
lines.show: Because it's sorted, the database doesn't start at the top. It *jumps* straight to the *S* section, narrows it down in [a few hops,] and lands on your exact row.

lines.say: Like the index in a book: find the word, get the page, skip the rest.
lines.show: It works like the index in a book: find the word, get the page, [skip the rest.]

lines.say: The catch? Every index takes space, and makes saving new users a bit slower, because each index must be updated too. So index what you search by, not everything.
lines.show: But there's a catch. Every index takes up *space,* and makes saving new users a bit *slower,* because each index must be updated too. So index [what you search by,] not everything.

lines.say: Postgres and MySQL index your primary key for you, usually the ID. Search by email, or anything else? Make sure it has its own index.
lines.show: *Postgres* and *MySQL* index your *primary key* for you, usually the ID. Search by email, or anything else? [Make sure it has its own index.]
